options: Components each on their own separate branch
All components on one single loop
questions.explanation: In parallel, each component rides its own branch between shared rails.
questions.misconception: Beads-on-one-string is the series layout, not parallel.

questions.prompt: A 3 V battery feeds three equal bulbs in parallel. About how many volts does each branch bulb see?
questions.explanation: Every branch connects straight across the battery, so each sees the full 3 V.
questions.misconception: Splitting the volts is what series does — parallel shares the source, not the voltage.

questions.prompt: You unscrew one bulb from a parallel circuit. The other bulbs...
questions.explanation: Independent branches mean the other lamps keep their own complete paths.
questions.misconception: That one-break-stops-all behavior is the signature of series circuits.

questions.prompt: Compared with the current on any single branch, the total current leaving the battery is...
options: The sum of all the branch currents
Exactly the same as one branch
questions.explanation: Current splits at the junction and recombines; the total equals the sum of parts.
questions.misconception: Current does not 'spend' at the first load — the junction just re-distributes it.

questions.prompt: Why do homes wire lights in parallel instead of series?
options: So one bulb failing doesn't black out every room
questions.explanation: Independent branches keep every other light working when any one fails.
questions.misconception: Series would doom the whole house to a single filament — that's why it's rejected.
